interfaces.interface_notes: In austenite-based duplex low-density steels the main crack sources originate from FCC/BCC (γ/α) interfaces. The paper reports that fine cracks at the γ/α interface (from detachment of α around voids) act as crack initiation sites specifically for the cryogenic (LNT) impact sample; for the RT impact sample a large number of subordinate cracks and large necking were observed.
interfaces.phase_evolution: No phase transformation of austenite during impact at RT (or LNT); the phase fractions remain stable.

structures.overall_structure: After RT impact testing, the steel retains its austenite-based duplex structure with no phase transformation in the austenite. In the crack-propagation zone near the fracture surface the deformation microstructure consists of dislocation cells or cell blocks (similar to tensile deformation), together with a small amount of deformation twinning and possible microbands.

unmapped_findings: Instrumented RT Charpy impact decomposition (Fig. 2(c)): crack initiation energy Wm = 79.28 J and crack propagation energy Wp = 251.33 J at RT; total impact energy 331 ± 4 J. Crack initiation energy is essentially the same (~80–100 J) at RT and LNT, while the crack propagation energy falls from 251 J (RT) to 156 J (LNT), meaning the RT Charpy impact is governed by crack-propagation energy.

Appearance of the RT impact fracture (Fig. 9(a)): a large number of subordinate cracks and large necking are seen, which the authors attribute to the high crack-propagation energy at room temperature (smaller necking and fewer subordinate cracks occur in the cryogenic sample).
The RT impact fracture surface is mainly composed of dimples of micrometer/sub-micrometer size (Fig. 9(e)), indicating ductile fracture at RT (and also at LNT).

Impact energy is reduced by about 30 % from 331 J at RT to 254 J at LNT, attributed to the presence of 3.0 % α-phase in the austenite matrix; the γ/α interface acts as a crack initiation site for the cryogenic (LNT) impact sample.
No phase transformation occurs in the austenite during impact deformation at either RT or LNT (the austenite is highly stable), as shown by EBSD phase maps near the fracture surfaces.
